rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: In Sufi thought, humans are wholly poor before God and depend on Him for existence and sustenance, while God is wholly self-sufficient.
rows.anchor: with regard to being both brought into existence and provided sustenance (Aj).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Realizing God's fullness or richness depends on realizing one's complete poverty before Him.
rows.anchor: realizing the Fullness or Richness of God depends upon the realization of one’s complete poverty before God.

rows.speaker: al-Tustarī
rows.claim: Al-Tustarī says God ordained servants' poverty in relation to Him; claiming wealth veils one from God, while acknowledging poverty joins the servant's poverty to God's wealth.

rows.speaker: al-Tustarī
rows.claim: The servant should feel inward poverty and cut off all besides God so servanthood is pure humility and abasement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Need for God is intrinsic to human nature, while need for other things is accidental; one should turn away from all besides God.
rows.anchor: poverty toward and need for God is intrinsic to human nature, whereas poverty toward or need for other things is accidental.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every experienced need is ultimately a need for God, since the things needed both veil Him and reveal Him.
rows.anchor: every need that one experiences is ultimately a need for God, since the phenomena for which one experiences need are veils that hide God and also reveal God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's being praised is intrinsic to the Divine Nature and does not depend on anyone praising Him.
rows.anchor: being praised is intrinsic to the Divine Nature and not dependent upon anything to praise Him.

rows.speaker: al-Maybudī
rows.claim: Al-Maybudī says only those who fully realize their poverty truly praise God.
rows.anchor: al-Maybudī states that only those who fully realize poverty truly praise God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to give the Quraysh an example of the fate of people who treated earlier message bearers as they were treating him.
rows.anchor: provide the Quraysh with an example of the fate that befell those who treated previous message bearers as they were treating him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening phrase of verse 13 can also be rendered, “Set forth for them a parable, the people of the town.”
rows.anchor: The first phrase of v. 13 could also be rendered, “Set forth for them a parable, the people of the town.”

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators identify the town as Antioch, though the source says this identification cannot be verified.
rows.anchor: Most identify the town as Antioch (IK, Q, Ṭ, Ṭs), though this identification cannot be verified (IK).

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators take the message bearers, called mursalīn rather than rusul, to be apostles whom Jesus sent to the town.
rows.anchor: Most commentators view the message bearers ( mursalīn, rather than rusul,“messengers”) as apostles sent to the town by Jesus.

rows.speaker: Most commentators
rows.claim: In the apostles interpretation, God's sending them means Jesus was commanded by God to send them.
rows.anchor: that God is said to have sent them indicates that Jesus was commanded by God to send them (Q, Ṭs).

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Commentators report that the townspeople beat and imprisoned the first two message bearers.
rows.anchor: After the first two were sent, the people of the town beat and imprisoned them (Q, Ṭ, Ṭs).

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some say the king ordered the punishment of the first two, after which a third message bearer was sent.
rows.anchor: Some say this punishment was ordered by the king (Aj), after which a third message bearer,

rows.speaker: Some
rows.claim: Some identify the third message bearer as Jonas.
rows.anchor: a third message bearer, whom some identify as Jonas, was sent.

rows.speaker: Another opinion
rows.claim: Another opinion identifies the message bearers as prophets, rather than apostles sent by a prophet.
rows.anchor: According to another opinion, the message bearers are prophets (Aj, Ṭs) rather than apostles sent by a prophet.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author finds the prophets interpretation more likely: Muhammad is called a mursal in 36:3 and 2:252, and other prophets are called mursalūn in many verses.
rows.anchor: This interpretation seems more likely, as the Prophet Muhammad is referred to as a mursal (message bearer) in v. 3 and in 2:252

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The declaration here and in verse 16 may also be translated, “we are message bearers unto you.”
rows.anchor: We have been sent unto you here and in v. 16 could also be rendered, “we are message bearers unto you.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers reply to the message bearers that they see an ill omen in them or foretell punishment that will befall them.
rows.anchor: This is the response of the disbelievers to the message bearers, meaning, “We see an ill omen or foretell a punishment that will befall you.”

rows.claim: The drop from which the human is created means sperm, also described elsewhere as a draught of base fluid.

rows.claim: For further discussion of human creation see 32:7–11, and for the stages of gestation see 22:5 and 23:14.

rows.claim: Failing to recognize one's own creation and what it testifies to makes one a manifest adversary to oneself.
